intro: Today's AI news is dominated by frontier-lab economics and infrastructure spending — Anthropic's IPO filing and Microsoft's headcount-for-datacenters trade reveal the scale of the compute buildout — alongside a notable policy alignment on web scraping and fresh evidence on AI security risks.

stories.title: Anthropic files for an IPO, revealing frontier-lab economics
stories.what_happened: Anthropic's IPO filing (S-1) discloses $16.29 billion in first-half 2026 revenue against $2.38 billion in cost of revenue, an 85% gross margin, with almost all costs tied to compute and infrastructure. The filing reveals roughly $750 billion in computing commitments, including up to $120.5 billion to SpaceX's AI subsidiary through 2029, and describes a history of operating in a compute-constrained environment.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the most detailed public look yet at how a frontier AI lab's unit economics actually work, showing massive revenue growth paired with even more massive forward compute commitments that dwarf current revenue. It gives investors, regulators, and competitors a template for evaluating whether AI labs are genuinely profitable businesses or compute-financing vehicles, and will likely set the benchmark against which OpenAI's and others' disclosures are judged.
stories.watch_next: Watch for how public markets price Anthropic's IPO once it prices, and whether rivals like OpenAI face pressure to disclose similarly granular compute-cost breakdowns.
stories.summary: Anthropic's IPO filing (S-1) discloses $16.29 billion in first-half 2026 revenue against $2.38 billion in cost of revenue, an 85% gross margin, with almost all costs tied to compute and infrastructure. The filing reveals roughly $750 billion in computing commitments, including up to $120.5 billion to SpaceX's AI subsidiary through 2029, and describes a history of operating in a compute-constrained environment.

stories.title: OpenAI reportedly raises $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
stories.what_happened: Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic are backing a unified robots.txt-style signal that lets publishers block AI scraping across all four platforms simultaneously. The move comes amid mounting legal pressure over unauthorized training-data collection.
stories.why_it_matters: A shared opt-out standard across the four largest AI developers would be the first coordinated industry response to publisher and rights-holder complaints about scraping, potentially reducing the patchwork of lawsuits and site-specific blocking rules that have proliferated over the past two years. It signals the industry anticipates further regulatory and legal scrutiny of training-data sourcing and wants to self-regulate before mandates arrive.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether publishers and news organizations adopt the standard widely, and whether smaller AI labs or Chinese model developers agree to honor it.
stories.summary: Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic are backing a unified robots.txt-style signal that lets publishers block AI scraping across all four platforms simultaneously. The move comes amid mounting legal pressure over unauthorized training-data collection.

stories.title: Microsoft reportedly offers voluntary severance to fund AI infrastructure
stories.what_happened: Microsoft is offering voluntary severance packages to roughly a quarter of its workforce — about 60,000 employees — while protecting AI-critical teams from cuts. The reallocated capital is intended to help fund a $170 billion AI infrastructure buildout.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the clearest signals yet that a major tech company is restructuring its entire workforce strategy around AI infrastructure spending, treating headcount reduction as a direct funding mechanism for data centers rather than a response to weak demand elsewhere. It underscores how capital-intensive the AI buildout has become and raises questions about whether other hyperscalers will follow with similar trade-offs between labor and compute investment.
stories.watch_next: Watch for Q4 earnings commentary on whether severance savings materially offset data center capex, and whether other hyperscalers announce comparable workforce-for-compute tradeoffs.
stories.summary: Microsoft is offering voluntary severance packages to roughly a quarter of its workforce — about 60,000 employees — while protecting AI-critical teams from cuts. The reallocated capital is intended to help fund a $170 billion AI infrastructure buildout.

stories.title: Moonshot restricts new API-user access to its Kimi K2 model series
stories.what_happened: SemiAnalysis benchmark data published October 31 shows AMD's MI355X serves Moonshot's 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model at $0.077 per million tokens versus $0.179 on Nvidia's B200 at 100 tokens/sec per user — about 2.3x cheaper. The gap narrows to $0.146 vs $0.275 at higher throughput, with the advantage attributed to the MI355X's larger HBM capacity and kernel-level tuning.
stories.why_it_matters: Independent, third-party benchmarks showing AMD meaningfully undercutting Nvidia on inference cost-per-token for a large open model are rare and significant, given Nvidia's near-total dominance of AI inference infrastructure. If these results hold up at scale, they could accelerate multi-vendor chip strategies among hyperscalers and give large open-weight model providers like Moonshot leverage to negotiate better hosting economics.
stories.watch_next: Watch for hyperscaler adoption announcements of MI355X at scale and whether Nvidia responds with pricing or performance updates for B200 successors.

stories.title: Brazilian Court Sanctions Lawyers for Prompt Injection in Court Filing
stories.what_happened: A Brazilian labor court censured and fined two lawyers for intentionally embedding a hidden prompt-injection command in a court filing, aiming to manipulate the AI system courts use to review filings. This may be the first judicial ruling globally to formally address intentional prompt-injection manipulation of a court's AI system.
stories.why_it_matters: As courts, governments, and businesses increasingly deploy AI to review documents and filings, this ruling establishes real-world legal precedent that prompt injection against institutional AI systems is sanctionable misconduct, not just a theoretical security concern. It signals that legal systems are beginning to treat AI manipulation attempts with the same seriousness as other forms of court interference or fraud.
stories.watch_next: Watch for similar cases in other jurisdictions and whether bar associations or court systems issue formal guidance on AI-filing manipulation as a professional-conduct violation.
stories.summary: A Brazilian labor court censured and fined two lawyers for intentionally embedding a hidden prompt-injection command in a court filing, aiming to manipulate the AI system courts use to review filings. This may be the first judicial ruling globally to formally address intentional prompt-injection manipulation of a court's AI system.
